blog_summary: Adrian Colyer introduces the Drinking Philosophers Problem by Chandy & Misra (1984), a paradigm for modeling conflict resolution in distributed systems. The paper addresses how to handle mutually exclusive actions when multiple processes compete for shared resources, emphasizing the need for distinguishability among conflicting processes to avoid unfair or deterministic deadlocks. The authors propose a solution using a directed graph (H) where processes (philosophers) have precedence based on edge directions, ensuring acyclicity and fairness through dynamic edge redirection. The blog highlights the elegance of the approach, which combines local decisions with global constraints, and its applicability to problems like graph-parallel computation (e.g., PowerGraph). The solution is symmetric, economic in message passing, and supports concurrent operations while avoiding probabilistic methods.

The Drinking Philosophers Problem
K. M. CHANDY and J. MISRA
University of Texas at Austin

The problem of resolving conflicts between processes in distributed systems is of practical importance.
A conflict between a set of processes must be resolved in favor of some (usually one) process and
